title: Blady grass and the grasses
scientificName: Imperata cylindrica; with Heteropogon contortus and Themeda triandra

identification.basis: The dictionary has general grass words but no word glossed 'blady grass'. Roth recorded blady grass (Imperata) as thatch, dilly-bag fibre and fish-fence material from Cape Bedford to the Tully, and Anderson records grass thatch, bags, sponges, ropes, bedding and signs at Bloomfield. Blady grass is not in the 30 km Karma Waters records; black speargrass and kangaroo grass are.

summary: **[jikan](word:jikan)** is grass, and **[kakarr](word:kakarr)** is 'grass; blanket to lie on, not to put over you', which says what grass was for first [ref:hershberger1982]. Blady grass, *Imperata cylindrica*, is the tall, sharp-edged, rhizome-forming grass of damp flats and creek margins, 'regarded as an excellent plant for thatching the roofs of traditional homes throughout south-east Asia', and in North Queensland the thatch of the [beehive hut](entry:huts-and-shelters), the fibre of Cape Bedford dilly bags, the weave of the fish-fence wings, and the toy spears of small boys [ref:wiki-imperata] [ref:roth1910-huts] [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1902]. The dictionary's grass words cover the rest of the grass toolkit: **[mawu](word:mawu)** 'a coarse grass used in the making of dilly bags', **[bilanji](word:bilanji)** 'grass used to make dilly bags', **[balji](word:balji)** the 'ladies' dilly bag, made from grass', **[wuju](word:wuju)** 'sponge made from grass, used as a sop for eating honey or soup', **[duburan](word:duburan)** the directional sign of 'grass twisted to point the way', **[warrbi](word:warrbi)** 'house made of grass', **[duli](word:duli)** 'burnt patch of grass' and **[jumul-jumul](word:jumul-jumul)** 'the grass seeds that get stuck in clothes, which come during the wet season' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[jikan](word:jikan)** 'grass'; **[kakarr](word:kakarr)** 'grass; blanket to lie on, not to put over you; also used as year, i.e. *kararr jambul* "two years"'; **[kararr](word:kararr)** 'a blanket, sheet, or grass bedding spread out to lie on'; **[kumul](word:kumul)** 'species of grass'; **[mawu](word:mawu)** 'a coarse grass used in the making of dilly bags'; **[bilanji](word:bilanji)** 'grass used to make dilly bags'; **[balji](word:balji)** 'ladie's dilly bag, made from grass or black palm'; **[wuju](word:wuju)** 'sponge made from grass'; **[duburan](word:duburan)** 'directional sign ... as a heap of stones or grass twisted to point the way; ring of soft materials to put on women's [heads] for carrying things'; **[warrbi](word:warrbi)** 'house made of grass, "beehive house"'; **[duli](word:duli)** 'burnt patch of grass'; **[jumul-jumul](word:jumul-jumul)** the clinging grass seeds of the wet; **[ngalku](word:ngalku)** 'bush fire' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Cape Bedford (Guugu Yimithirr) word *dirnbur* was both the blady grass and the dilly-bag made from it, 'the name of the plant itself' [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1901-string]. The Bloomfield bag grass that Roth and Anderson name is not blady grass but *Lomandra* (then *Xerotes*), *mau-u*, which the [dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) page covers [ref:roth1901-string] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Blady grass, speargrass, kangaroo grass
sections.body:
**Blady grass**, *Imperata cylindrica*, 'is a species of perennial rhizomatous grass'. It 'grows from 0.2–3 m tall, its stalk is firm and has nodes covered with long white hairs. Each clump that grows shares an extensive rhizome network'; 'the leaves are about 2 cm wide in average and 12–80 centimetres in length near the base of the plant and narrow to a sharp point at the top; the margins are finely toothed and are embedded with sharp silica crystals'; the seed heads are narrow white plumes. 'It spreads both through small seeds, which are easily carried by the wind, and rhizomes'. It 'is a pyrophyte. It is highly flammable, even when still apparently green, particularly in tropical climates' [ref:wiki-imperata]. The blade is the 'blade' of the name; Roth knew it as *Imperata arundinacea*, 'Blady Grass' [ref:roth1904].

**Black speargrass** (*Heteropogon contortus*) and **kangaroo grass** (*Themeda triandra*) are the grasses of the dry inland woodland under the ironbarks and bloodwoods, with their twisted awns and their seed that the finches and the fires live on; the [woodland](entry:woodland) page has them [ref:wiki-heteropogon] [ref:wiki-themeda] [ref:re-woodland].

**Grass in Roth's North Queensland.** The thatch of the beehive hut was 'bark, blady-grass, lawyer-vine, cycad- or palm-leaf according to the local vegetation', and on the lower Tully the grass was laid 'two and a half to three feet long' in handfuls, butts down then butts up, fixed with a spiral of split cane [ref:roth1910-huts]. At Cape Bedford 'the long leaves, dried in the sun, are put into fresh water, and split. These lengths are made up into dilly-bags, which are called *dirnbur*', and the sieve-baskets were 'woven from twine derived from *Haemodorum coccineum*, *Spinifex hirsutus*, *Imperata arundinacea* ("Blady Grass"), etc.' [ref:roth1904]. In the eel-trap fences of the coast, sticks were 'driven in vertically, and plenty of big blady-grass intertwined, so as to prevent the fish passing through anywhere, except into the trap', and the flood-time net wings were 'short thin stakes intertwined with blady grass' [ref:roth1901]. Small boys' 'toy spears are thus made from light thin withes or else from grasses, reeds, and rushes, e.g., *Andropogon*, *Imperata*' [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: Which grass for which job
sections.body:
- **Blady grass**: wide flat blades, white plumes, damp flats; thatch, bag fibre, fish fences [ref:wiki-imperata] [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1901].
- **Speargrass**: tall, with the black twisted awns that drill into socks and skin in the late dry; the fire grass of the woodland; its stems are sucked for sweet sap in the Northern Territory [ref:wiki-heteropogon].
- **Kangaroo grass**: the rusty-headed tussock grass; seed ground for bread and stems twisted for string elsewhere in Australia [ref:wiki-themeda].
- **Lomandra** (*mau-u*), a grass-like lily: the Bloomfield bag grass; see [dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) [ref:roth1901-string] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Reeds** of the river bed (*Phragmites*): the reed-spear shafts of the Mitchell, 'cut green, and stored in large quantities', straightened in the fire [ref:palmer1883].
- **Spinifex** (*Triodia*) on the stoniest ground, the resin grass; see [beeswax and gums](entry:beeswax-and-gums) [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **A knotted tussock with its tips pointing**, a stem woven into a shrub, straws tied to a tree: *duburan*, a message on the path, saying who went where and how many, or where the water or the food is [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Burnt patches** (*duli*) and green pick: the managed woodland, and where the [wallabies](entry:wallaby) will be [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:re-woodland].
- **Flattened grass beds** and grass bundles in a half-ring: a camp [ref:roth1910-huts] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Round woven grass nests** with a tube entrance high in a gum: the black-throated finch [ref:wiki-btf].
- **Seeds in your socks** in the wet: *jumul-jumul* [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Where the grasses grow
sections.body: Blady grass wants moisture: damp flats, creek margins, the edges of swamps, and it holds ground with its rhizome mat, which is why it is planted 'for ground cover and soil stabilization' elsewhere [ref:wiki-imperata]. The Tully, the Bloomfield and Cape Bedford, where Roth saw it used, are wet coastal country [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910-huts].

sections.heading: Grass, fire and seed
sections.body: The grass is the fuel and the feed of the whole [woodland](entry:woodland): kangaroo grass and speargrass feed the wallabies and the finches, carry the dry-season burns and come back green behind them [ref:wiki-themeda] [ref:wiki-heteropogon] [ref:re-woodland]. Blady grass is the extreme case, 'highly flammable, even when still apparently green', and it is the rhizome that survives the fire and the dense mat and the chemicals it releases that let it 'outcompete' other plants [ref:wiki-imperata]. The [fire-drive](entry:hunting-with-fire) and the cultural burn are grass management; the dictionary's *duli* and *ngalku* are the vocabulary of it [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:pbg-cape-york].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Thatch and bag grass are cut long in the late wet and early dry, when the blades are full length; bedding grass whenever the camp moves; the seeds that stick in clothes come 'during the wet season'; the burns run from the early dry as the grass cures, 'every 2–5 years' in the ironbark-bloodwood woodland [ref:roth1910-huts] [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:re-woodland] [ref:pbg-cape-york]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Thatch** for the beehive hut, laid from the top down in handfuls fixed with cane [ref:roth1910-huts].
- **Dilly bags and sieve-baskets** from sun-dried, soaked, split blades (Cape Bedford) [ref:roth1904].
- **Fish-fence wings** of stakes with blady grass woven through [ref:roth1901].
- **Bedding**: *kararr*, bunches of long grass as a mattress [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Windbreaks** of grass bundles round the sleeping place [ref:roth1910-huts].
- **Sponges** (*wuju*) for honey and soup, and for swirling fish poison [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Grass ropes** for climbing to high bee nests [ref:anderson1996].
- **Tinder** for the fire-drill [ref:anderson1996].
- **A brush** for sorting zamia flour [ref:anderson1996].
- **Signs** on the path, *duburan* [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Head rings** of grass for carrying, the Cape Bedford *mordi* [ref:roth1910] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Toy spears** for boys [ref:roth1902].
- **Necklaces** of grass-stem bugles [ref:anderson1996].
- **Seed** of other grasses ground for bread in the west [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Grass work
sections.body:
**Thatching a hut** (lower Tully method, Roth) [ref:roth1910-huts]: cut blady grass two and a half to three feet long; lay handfuls butts-down against the frame all round, then a layer butts-up, and tie both on with a split cane run round the hut; then single rows, each tied with cane, spiralling up; cap the top with teatree bark or palm leaves; weigh it with logs. Put on plenty: the rain is kept out by the quantity, not the arrangement [ref:roth1910-huts]. The frame is on the [huts](entry:huts-and-shelters) page.

**A grass dilly bag** (Cape Bedford, Roth) [ref:roth1904]: dry the long blades in the sun; soak them in fresh water; split them into strands; work them up on the bag's mesh. The mesh patterns are on the [dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) page.

**A fish-fence wing** [ref:roth1901]: drive thin stakes in a V from the trap's mouth and weave big blady grass through them so nothing passes except into the trap; see [fish traps](entry:fish-traps).

**A grass sponge** (*wuju*) [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996]: pull two or three handfuls, take off the roots, rub the grass hard between the hands until it is a soft pad; sop honey or soup with it, or wrap the mashed fish-poison seed in it and swirl it under water.

**A bed**: a shallow hollow in the sand, bunches of long grass laid thick, a paperbark sheet over you in the cold; see [bark blankets](entry:bark-blankets) [ref:anderson1996].

**A sign**: knot a tussock with its tips pointing the way you went, or weave a stem into a shrub, butt as the pointer [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Blady grass cuts: the blade edges carry silica crystals [ref:wiki-imperata].
- It burns green; a grass fire in cured speargrass in the late dry moves faster than a person; permits apply [ref:wiki-imperata] [ref:re-woodland] [ref:qfd].
- Dry grass bedding and a fire are a hut fire; see [huts](entry:huts-and-shelters) [ref:roth1910-huts].
- Never a hand into long grass you cannot see into; see [snakes](entry:snakes) [ref:re-woodland].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Grass is the one material that is always there and always free, and most of what this page lists can be tried on a river camp in an afternoon: a sponge, a bed, a sign on the path, a windbreak [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982]. What each people calls its grasses, and which grass it used for what, is for the contribution box below.

locations.summary: Blady grass is barely on the record around the Hann: the Atlas of Living Australia holds just 2 records, from 1970 and 2023, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru, against 10 of black speargrass and 18 of kangaroo grass [ref:ala-hann-grass]. The Hann's woodland has 'a ground cover of coarse grasses such as speargrass' [ref:wp-hann]. Kuku Thaypan Elders call the grasses together **Kwern**, and read them as the calendar for burning [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Where the grasses are here
sections.body: Along the Hann the trees are stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark 'with a ground cover of coarse grasses such as speargrass' [ref:wp-hann]. Open grassy plains, **Kwern**, are one of the nine kinds of country the Kuku Thaypan Elders name [ref:standley2019]. Blady grass wants damp ground; with only two Atlas records near the river, the grasses that matter here are the speargrasses, cockatoo grass and kangaroo grass [ref:ala-hann-grass] [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Grass and the year here
sections.body: Kuku Thaypan Elders read the grass to time their fires. In the early dry, which on the south-eastern side of Cape York is 'usually in April or May', 'Kwern umbayal Tall Spear grass (Heteropogan triticius) seed stalks begin to fall down and native grass seed begin to be knocked off the plants by the rain, making them ready for fire, smoke and germination' [ref:standley2019]. In their calendar the cockatoo grass, **Kwern yulan**, has 'finished flowering and fruiting' before the burns begin, and black speargrass is seeding as the grasses cure [ref:standley2019]. Messmate country is ready to burn 'when Eriachne sp is setting seed and bark has shed' [ref:standley2019]. After the wet, the giant speargrass's 'root base is a vital source of nutritious moisture' [ref:standley2019]. See [hunting with fire](entry:hunting-with-fire).

sections.heading: How people used grass here
sections.body:
**Kuku Thaypan Elders.** Cockatoo or sugarbag grass, *Kwern Yulan*, 'was used in medicines and its root base was used as a mop in the collection of sugarbag or native honey' [ref:standley2019]. See [native bees](entry:native-bees).

**Princess Charlotte Bay hinterland and the Palmer, c. 1900.** A duck hunter covered 'his head with a bundle of long grass, tied about near to its extremities into something like a horse-collar', and stalked through the water looking 'like a tussock of grass floating down the stream' [ref:roth1901].

**Morehead and Musgrave rivers, c. 1900.** For spinning human-hair twine, the spindle was 'about 8 in. long, and made from a piece of grass-stem' [ref:roth1901-string].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country [ref:fca-possum] and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, both determined in November 2023 [ref:fca-thaypan]. Where the Thaypan rights are non-exclusive, they include the right to light fires 'for cultural, spiritual or domestic purposes including cooking, but not for the purpose of hunting or clearing vegetation' [ref:fca-thaypan].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: Kuku Thaypan (Awu Alaya) words recorded with the Elders: **Kwern** grasses in general; **Kwern umbayal** giant spear grass (*Heteropogon triticeus*); **Kwern Yulan** cockatoo or sugarbag grass (*Alloteropsis semialata*); **Che giuill** wild rice (*Oryza*); **chigaru** reed grass [ref:standley2019]. These are Kuku Thaypan, not Kuku Yalanji.

locations.summary: At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the recorded grasses are black speargrass and kangaroo grass; blady grass is not in the 30 km records, and the methods here work with whatever long grass the flats give [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:wiki-heteropogon] [ref:wiki-themeda].

sections.heading: The grasses on the record here
sections.body: **Black speargrass** (*Heteropogon contortus*) and **kangaroo grass** (*Themeda triandra*) are the recorded grasses of the Karma Waters woodland, the ones under the ironbarks and bloodwoods, with their twisted awns and their seed that the finches and the fires live on; the [woodland](entry:woodland) page has them [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:wiki-heteropogon] [ref:wiki-themeda] [ref:re-woodland].

sections.heading: Where the grasses grow here
sections.body: Within 30 km of Karma Waters the Atlas records black speargrass and kangaroo grass, the grasses of the dry ironbark and bloodwood woodland on sand, and no blady grass; if it is here it is on the wetter ground by the river and the soaks [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:re-woodland].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Whether blady grass grows on the Karma Waters flats, and what the Western Yalanji call the speargrass and the kangaroo grass, is for the contribution box below [ref:ala-karma-plants].

locations.summary: On the Bloomfield, grass was the everyday stuff of camp: hut covering, mattresses, sponges, climbing ropes, tinder, bead necklaces and path signs [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Grass at Bloomfield
sections.body: Anderson: huts 'covered with whatever they could get nearest at hand, either the leaves of the Fan Palm, Lawyer Palms, grass or bark'; 'bunches of long bush grass served as mattresses on hard ground'; a 'grass sponge' swirled the *Barringtonia* fish poison into the water; 'when the nests were high in the tree, grass ropes were made for climbing'; the fire-drill's ember 'caught alight with the addition of dry grass and wood particles'; zamia flour was separated 'with a small grass brush'; 'necklaces of grass-bugles' were worn; and the path signs, *duburan*, ranged 'from a knotted tussock of grass with the tips pointing in the desired direction, a single stem of grass woven into the branches of a shrub, a number of straws or a palm leaf tied to a tree (all with their butts as pointers), to rather complicated little devices tied to sticks pushed into the ground' [ref:anderson1996].
